newsitem.title: USA: Deal talks will not delay Fla Medicaid trial - judge.
newsitem.headline: Deal talks will not delay Fla Medicaid trial - judge.

text.p: The judge in Florida's $1 billion Medicaid case against the U.S. tobacco industry said on Friday sweeping secret settlement talks on cigarette litigation would not delay an August start of a jury trial in the lawsuit.

"It should be clear to all parties, counsel, and the appellate court that alleged 'secret settlement negotiations' will have absolutely no effect on the commencement of trial in this case ...," Palm Beach County Circuit Court Judge Harold Cohen wrote in a decision.
Cohen said the scheduled August 1 start of jury selection could only be derailed by an out-of-court settlement and dismissal of the lawsuit by the state of Florida.
The judge made the statement in a written decision authorizing the release of some Liggett Group documents to Florida's attorneys. Liggett is a unit of Brooke Group Ltd.
A pool of 300 potential jurors is being summoned, and court schedules are being r-arranged to allow for the high-profile trial, which is expected to last three or four months, Cohen wrote.

News of the talks, which involve tobacco companies, attorneys general of Florida and other states and other anti-tobacco activists, broke on Wednesday. Talks are expected to resume on Sunday in Chicago, people close to the talks said.
Published reports have said tobacco companies might agree to pay as much as $300 billion over 25 years into a compensation fund for smokers who fall sick with lung cancer and other diseases.

In return, the tobacco industry would be granted broad shelter from lawsuits, including those filed by the attorneys general seeking compensation for an estimated $30 billion spent by states treating sick smokers.

Florida's lawsuit to recover Medicaid costs is one of the first of 23 scheduled to come to trial. It is being closely watched because Florida has a special law that undoes many of the industry's stand-by defenses against liability claims.
The state has also won the right to press for punitive damages and collect still more if it can show the tobacco companies violated anti-racketeering laws.
